Rhododendron cumberlandense is an Appalachian native deciduous azalea producing vivid orange-red to deep red, funnel-shaped, mildly fragrant flowers in early to midsummer, well after the spring flush of most other native azaleas has finished, extending the native azalea bloom season into summer. Its late timing and fiery flower color make it a valuable addition to a native shrub border or open woodland garden planned for a long succession of bloom, and it tolerates the acidic, well-drained mountain soils typical of its native range. Give it consistently moist but well-drained, acidic soil and dappled shade, avoiding both deep shade, which reduces flowering, and hot, dry, exposed sites.

Rhododendron colemanii is a large, vigorous deciduous azalea only formally described in 2008 from the Red Hills region of Alabama and Georgia, producing intensely fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers in shades of cream, pale pink, orange, and yellow in late spring to early summer, with considerable variation in color among individual plants. As a genuine Gulf South native azalea, it is exceptionally well suited to zone 8–9 gardens where many other native azaleas struggle with heat and humidity, making it an excellent choice for a naturalized woodland border in the Deep South. It tolerates more heat than mountain-native azaleas but still needs consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil and the dappled light of a high pine or hardwood canopy to perform well.

Rhododendron eastmanii is a South Carolina native deciduous azalea producing clean white to pale pink, sweetly fragrant flowers in mid to late spring, later than the similar Piedmont azalea it was once confused with, and is one of the more recently recognized species in the eastern native azalea complex. Its clear white flowers and strong fragrance make it a choice addition to a native plant collection or woodland garden focused on regional biodiversity, and it associates well with other native azaleas, oakleaf hydrangea, and understory dogwoods. Give it the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and filtered light favored by other native deciduous azaleas.

Rhododendron minus is a compact, evergreen southeastern native with small, leathery, dark green leaves and clusters of pink to rose-purple, funnel-shaped flowers in late spring to early summer, occurring naturally on dry rocky slopes and bluffs from the Carolinas into the Gulf South. Its smaller stature and greater heat and drought tolerance compared with the large-leaved mountain rhododendrons make it one of the more practical evergreen rhododendrons for lowland southeastern gardens, including well-drained Gulf Coast sites with some afternoon shade. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and avoid heavy, poorly drained clay, which this species tolerates poorly despite otherwise being one of the tougher rhododendron species for the Deep South.

Rhododendron chapmanii is a federally listed endangered evergreen shrub found only in a handful of sandhill and scrub sites in the Florida Panhandle and southwest Georgia, with small, leathery leaves and clusters of rose-pink, funnel-shaped flowers in early to mid-spring. Unlike most rhododendrons, it is naturally adapted to sharply drained, sandy soil and considerable sun exposure, making it more drought-tolerant than typical evergreen rhododendrons and a good candidate for a well-drained Gulf Coast native garden. Growing this rare species in cultivation from nursery-propagated stock helps support conservation of the species by reducing pressure on its few remaining wild populations, so buy only from reputable native-plant nurseries with documented cultivated origin.
